text: Nearly every ML algorithm's internals are built entirely on numbers. A column full of the strings "basic," "standard," "premium" has no numeric meaning a model can use directly. Encoding turns category labels into numbers — and which encoding you pick has real consequences.

One-hot encoding creates a new binary column for every category, with exactly one set to 1 per row. This avoids implying any order between categories — standard isn't mathematically "more" than basic just because you encoded it that way.

Ordinal encoding is different: it compresses categories into a single numeric column that preserves a real order, like low, medium, high. Use it on a column with no real order, like plan or region, and you invent a false numeric relationship that doesn't exist.

So the choice comes down to one question: does a real order exist? If yes, ordinal. If no, one-hot. And if there are thousands of distinct values, like zip codes, one-hot explodes into thousands of columns, and other techniques exist outside this course's scope.

And the same trap from the last two lessons applies here too: fit the encoder on the training set only, so it learns the category set from train, then use that exact same fitted encoder to transform test — never refit on the full dataset.
Next, we close out this chapter with the problem that connects back to nearly every "fit on train only" rule you've seen so far: data leakage.
